docs.title: HTTPX Tenacity
docs.text: A lightweight package that provides tenacious (retrying) httpx and httpx2 transports.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The package is published on PyPI. Plain pip install httpx-tenacity installs only the shared core with the retry policies, which contains no HTTP client. Select the HTTP client you use with an extra, httpx or httpx2.

pip install 'httpx-tenacity[httpx]'
pip install 'httpx-tenacity[httpx2]'

To use both HTTP clients in the same process, install both extras.

pip install 'httpx-tenacity[httpx,httpx2]'

There is no automatic fallback: you choose the integration explicitly by importing from httpx_tenacity.httpx or from httpx_tenacity.httpx2. The retry policies, such as SmartRetryPolicy, are independent of the HTTP client and work with the transports of both integrations.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(policy=SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=3))
client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)

response = client.get("https://api.example.com/data")

import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(policy=SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=3))
client = httpx2.Client(transport=transport)

response = client.get("https://api.example.com/data")

The tutorial shows more examples, including the asynchronous transports.

docs.title: Migrating from <0.3
docs.text:
The transports moved out of the package root and httpx is no longer a required dependency. Install httpx-tenacity[httpx] instead of httpx-tenacity and change your imports. RetryPolicy, SmartRetryPolicy, and RetryingT keep their import paths.

-from httpx_tenacity import TenaciousTransport
+from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

The same applies to AsyncTenaciousTransport and HTTPXHTTPTransportKeywordArguments. For HTTPX2, import them from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 instead.

Additionally, create() takes a policy instead of the max_attempts, multiplier, max_wait_seconds, min_wait_seconds, and exponent_base arguments.

-transport = TenaciousTransport.create(max_attempts=3)
+transport = TenaciousTransport.create(policy=SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=3))

docs.title: Retry policies
docs.text:
The following symbols are exposed to the user by the client-independent package root:

  • RetryPolicy
  • SmartRetryPolicy
  • RetryingT

The following helpers, which the default policy is built from, are client-independent as well. They are not exported by the package root, so import them from their own modules:

  • smart_wait from httpx_tenacity.wait
  • is_server_side_issue from httpx_tenacity.retry_callback

docs.title: httpx_tenacity
docs.text:
Provide the retry policies that configure the tenacious transports.

This package imports no HTTP client. The transports live in the integration packages, httpx_tenacity.httpx for HTTPX and httpx_tenacity.httpx2 for HTTPX2. Each of them requires its own extra.

docs.title: SmartRetryPolicy
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

Define the default retry policy.

The policy retries request errors and server-side issues. Between attempts, it waits for the time given in a response header when the response has one of the expected status codes, and otherwise uses random exponential backoff.

Attributes:

Name Type Description max_attempts int

Maximum number of attempts.

multiplier float

Multiplier for the exponential backoff between retries.

max_wait_seconds float | timedelta

Maximum wait time between retries.

min_wait_seconds float | timedelta

Minimum wait time between retries.

exponent_base float

The base for the exponential backoff.

status_code int | tuple[int, ...]

The response status code or codes whose header sets the wait.

header str

The response header that holds the wait time in seconds.

docs.title: httpx_tenacity.wait
docs.text: Provide custom wait functions.

docs.title: smart_wait
docs.text:
Bases: wait_random_exponential

Define a wait strategy that smartly backs-off.

This strategy first checks HTTP responses for an expected status code (by default 429) that indicates that the server is busy. If the status code matches, it checks the response header (by default 'Retry-After') for a wait time indication. Otherwise, it uses random exponential backoff.

docs.title: __call__(retry_state: tenacity.RetryCallState) -> float
docs.text:
Return a wait time in seconds based on response headers or retry state.

When we have a successful outcome, i.e., we received an HTTP response without encountering an exception, and the HTTP status code of the response matches the specified status code, check if the response header indicates a wait time; otherwise use the random exponential strategy to determine the wait time.

docs.title: is_server_side_issue(response: Response) -> bool
docs.text:
Return whether the response indicates a server side issue.

A server side issue is defined as either an HTTP server error code (500 - 599) or too many requests (429).

docs.title: TenaciousTransport
docs.text:
Bases: BaseTransport

Define the synchronous tenacious (retrying) transport.

This transport consists of a composed transport for handling requests and an appropriately configured tenacity retrying instance.

The transport owns the composed transport, including one that you pass in yourself. Entering, exiting, or closing this transport does the same to the composed transport, in the same way that httpx.Client treats its transport.

docs.text:
Create an instance of a synchronous tenacious (retrying) transport.

This factory method constructs the instance with an underlying httpx.HTTPTransport. That transport is passed any additional keyword arguments.

The retry policy creates the tenacity retrying instance. The default SmartRetryPolicy retries requests when there are server-side issues and will either wait the time set in a Retry-After response header or use a random exponential backoff.

The returned transport owns the underlying transport, including one passed in as transport, and closes it when it is closed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
httpx-tenacity adds automatic retry logic to HTTPX and HTTPX2. For each of the two HTTP clients, it provides two transport classes:

  • TenaciousTransport: Synchronous transport for blocking requests
  • AsyncTenaciousTransport: Asynchronous transport for async/await requests

You choose the integration explicitly by importing the transports from httpx_tenacity.httpx for HTTPX or from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 for HTTPX2. Each of them requires the matching extra, httpx or httpx2.

Every example below is shown for both HTTP clients. Pick the tab that matches the client you installed. Transports, clients, and responses must all come from the same client: httpx_tenacity.httpx works with httpx and httpx_tenacity.httpx2 works with httpx2. Mixing them fails.

Both transports, when created with the default factory, automatically retry requests when encountering server-side issues (HTTP 5xx errors and 429 Too Many Requests responses) using exponential backoff with optional Retry-After header support.

docs.title: Basic Setup
docs.text:
Create a client with automatic retry logic:

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create()
client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)

response = client.get("https://api.example.com/data")

import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create()
client = httpx2.Client(transport=transport)

response = client.get("https://api.example.com/data")

The create() method uses the default SmartRetryPolicy, which has sensible defaults:

  • Maximum 5 retry attempts
  • Exponential backoff with base 2
  • Minimum wait of 0.02 seconds between retries
  • Maximum wait of 60 seconds between retries
  • The wait time from the Retry-After header of 429 Too Many Requests responses

docs.title: Configuring Retry Behavior
docs.text:
Pass a configured policy when creating the transport:

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(
    policy=SmartRetryPolicy(
        max_attempts=10,  # Try up to 10 times
        multiplier=2,  # Exponential backoff multiplier
        min_wait_seconds=0.1,  # Minimum 0.1 second between retries
        max_wait_seconds=120,  # Maximum 2 minutes between retries
        exponent_base=2,  # Base for exponential calculation
        status_code=(429, 503),  # Responses whose header sets the wait time
        header="Retry-After",  # Header that holds the wait time in seconds
    ),
)
client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)

import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(
    policy=SmartRetryPolicy(
        max_attempts=10,  # Try up to 10 times
        multiplier=2,  # Exponential backoff multiplier
        min_wait_seconds=0.1,  # Minimum 0.1 second between retries
        max_wait_seconds=120,  # Maximum 2 minutes between retries
        exponent_base=2,  # Base for exponential calculation
        status_code=(429, 503),  # Responses whose header sets the wait time
        header="Retry-After",  # Header that holds the wait time in seconds
    ),
)
client = httpx2.Client(transport=transport)

A policy does not depend on the HTTP client. The same SmartRetryPolicy works with the synchronous and the asynchronous transport of both HTTPX and HTTPX2.

docs.title: Passing Transport Configuration
docs.text:
Additional keyword arguments are passed to the underlying transport of the selected client. The accepted keywords are described by HTTPXHTTPTransportKeywordArguments and HTTPX2HTTPTransportKeywordArguments. Types such as Limits and Proxy must come from the selected client.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(
    policy=SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=5),
    verify=False,  # Disable SSL verification
    limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=10),
)
client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)

import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport.create(
    policy=SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=5),
    verify=False,  # Disable SSL verification
    limits=httpx2.Limits(max_connections=10),
)
client = httpx2.Client(transport=transport)

docs.title: Monitoring Retries
docs.text:
Retries are logged at DEBUG level. Enable debug logging to see retry activity:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

The transports log to loggers named after their modules, for example httpx_tenacity.httpx.tenacious_transport and httpx_tenacity.httpx2.tenacious_transport.

docs.title: Custom Retry Policies
docs.text:
Any object with a create() method that matches the RetryPolicy protocol can replace the default policy. The transport calls it with the tenacity retrying class it needs, its HTTP client's request error, and its logger. Because the transport passes its own client's RequestError, one policy serves the transports of both clients:

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import logging

import tenacity
from httpx_tenacity import RetryingT
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport


class FixedRetryPolicy:
    def create(
        self,
        retrying_class: type[RetryingT],
        *,
        request_error: type[Exception],
        logger: logging.Logger,
    ) -> RetryingT:
        return retrying_class(
            retry=tenacity.retry_if_exception_type(request_error),
            stop=tenacity.stop_after_attempt(3),
            wait=tenacity.wait_fixed(1),
            before_sleep=tenacity.before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG),
            reraise=True,
        )


transport = TenaciousTransport.create(policy=FixedRetryPolicy())

import logging

import tenacity
from httpx_tenacity import RetryingT
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport


class FixedRetryPolicy:
    def create(
        self,
        retrying_class: type[RetryingT],
        *,
        request_error: type[Exception],
        logger: logging.Logger,
    ) -> RetryingT:
        return retrying_class(
            retry=tenacity.retry_if_exception_type(request_error),
            stop=tenacity.stop_after_attempt(3),
            wait=tenacity.wait_fixed(1),
            before_sleep=tenacity.before_sleep_log(logger, logging.DEBUG),
            reraise=True,
        )


transport = TenaciousTransport.create(policy=FixedRetryPolicy())

docs.title: Completely Custom Retry Logic
docs.text:
For full control over retry behavior, provide a custom tenacity Retrying instance together with the transport that handles the requests. In that case, you decide what to retry, so use the RequestError of the selected client: httpx.RequestError is not a subclass of httpx2.RequestError, and the other way around.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import httpx
from tenacity import Retrying, retry_if_exception_type, stop_after_attempt, wait_fixed
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport(
    retry=Retrying(
        retry=retry_if_exception_type(httpx.RequestError),
        stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
        wait=wait_fixed(1),
    ),
    transport=httpx.HTTPTransport(),
)
client = httpx.Client(transport=transport)

import httpx2
from tenacity import Retrying, retry_if_exception_type, stop_after_attempt, wait_fixed
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport

transport = TenaciousTransport(
    retry=Retrying(
        retry=retry_if_exception_type(httpx2.RequestError),
        stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
        wait=wait_fixed(1),
    ),
    transport=httpx2.HTTPTransport(),
)
client = httpx2.Client(transport=transport)

docs.title: Asynchronous Usage
docs.text:
The asynchronous transport works in an analogous manner and can be configured as described above for the synchronous transport. Retrying also works with concurrent requests over the same transport instance.

HTTPXHTTPX2 
import anyio
import httpx
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import AsyncTenaciousTransport


async def main():
    async with (
        httpx.AsyncClient(transport=AsyncTenaciousTransport.create()) as client,
        anyio.create_task_group() as tg,
    ):
        tg.start_soon(client.get, "https://api.example.com/data")
        tg.start_soon(client.post, "https://api.example.com/data")


anyio.run(main)

import anyio
import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import AsyncTenaciousTransport


async def main():
    async with (
        httpx2.AsyncClient(transport=AsyncTenaciousTransport.create()) as client,
        anyio.create_task_group() as tg,
    ):
        tg.start_soon(client.get, "https://api.example.com/data")
        tg.start_soon(client.post, "https://api.example.com/data")


anyio.run(main)

docs.title: Using Both Clients Together
docs.text:
You can install both extras, httpx-tenacity[httpx,httpx2], and use both integrations in the same process. The policy is independent of the HTTP client, so you may even share one policy between them. The HTTP objects, however, are not interchangeable: an httpx_tenacity.httpx transport cannot be used with an httpx2.Client, and an httpx_tenacity.httpx2 transport cannot be used with an httpx.Client.

import httpx
import httpx2
from httpx_tenacity import SmartRetryPolicy
from httpx_tenacity.httpx import TenaciousTransport as HTTPXTransport
from httpx_tenacity.httpx2 import TenaciousTransport as HTTPX2Transport

policy = SmartRetryPolicy(max_attempts=3)

with (
    httpx.Client(transport=HTTPXTransport.create(policy=policy)) as old,
    httpx2.Client(transport=HTTPX2Transport.create(policy=policy)) as new,
):
    first = old.get("https://api.example.com/data")  # an httpx.Response
    second = new.get("https://api.example.com/data")  # an httpx2.Response

docs.title: ADR001 - Adopt tenacity for retrying
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-01-11
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Implement retry behaviour for httpx transports on top of the tenacity library instead of writing custom retry logic. The sync and async transports delegate stop, wait, and retry conditions to tenacity.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: httpx has no built-in retry mechanism beyond connection-level retries on its HTTPTransport. The httpx issue requesting retries (encode/httpx#108) has drawn requests and workarounds from users since 2019, which shows a clear need among httpx users. Applications need retries for transient server-side failures, such as 5xx responses or 429 rate limiting. This has to work identically for sync and async clients. Writing and maintaining that logic by hand is error-prone and duplicates mature existing solutions.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) tenacity
  2. backoff
  3. urllib3 Retry
  4. httpx-retries
  5. stamina

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): tenacity
docs.text: A general-purpose retrying library with composable stop, wait, and retry strategies, used inside custom httpx transports.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: it is a mature, widely used library with composable stop, wait, and retry strategies and native support for both sync and async code.
  • Adopted because: it can be wrapped at the transport level, so retries apply to every request made through an httpx client.
  • Adopted despite: it adds a runtime dependency, and its general-purpose API needs adapting to httpx (custom retry callback and Retry-After-aware wait).
  • Adopted despite: its API is large and somewhat complex, so the transports wrap it in create() factories with sensible defaults.

docs.title: Option 2: backoff
docs.text: A decorator-based library for retrying with exponential backoff.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: it is built around function decorators, offering limited customisation and no natural fit at the httpx transport level.
  • Rejected despite: it is lightweight and supports both sync and async code.

docs.title: Option 3: urllib3 Retry
docs.text: urllib3's retry configuration, as used by requests through a mounted HTTPAdapter.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: it is tied to requests and urllib3, does not carry over to httpx transports, and offers limited customisation.
  • Rejected despite: it is well known, battle-tested, and handles Retry-After out of the box.

docs.title: Option 4: httpx-retries
docs.text: A retrying transport package for httpx.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: its retry and wait strategies offered too little customisation for the desired behaviour.
  • Rejected despite: it is purpose-built for httpx and already works at the transport level.

docs.title: Option 5: stamina
docs.text: An opinionated wrapper around tenacity with production-ready defaults.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: it deliberately hides most of tenacity's configuration, making it less flexible than using tenacity directly.
  • Rejected despite: it provides safe defaults and builds on the same proven retry engine.

docs.title: ADR002 - Use composition over inheritance
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-01-11
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The tenacious transports subclass only the abstract httpx.BaseTransport / httpx.AsyncBaseTransport and wrap an injected transport and a tenacity retrying instance, instead of subclassing httpx.HTTPTransport. Each request is delegated to the wrapped transport inside a fresh copy of the retrying loop.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: httpx separates clients from transports, and any object implementing httpx.BaseTransport or httpx.AsyncBaseTransport can be plugged into a client. Retrying is cross-cutting behaviour that should apply regardless of which transport sends the request: the default HTTPTransport, a MockTransport in tests, or third-party transports such as caching layers. It should also be possible to layer retrying with other wrapping transports in whatever order an application needs.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) Composition
  2. Subclass the HTTP transports

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): Composition
docs.text: Subclass only the abstract base transports and wrap an injected transport, delegating each request to it inside the retrying loop.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: it works with any transport implementing the base interface.
  • Adopted because: it can be stacked with other wrapping transports in any order.
  • Adopted because: the wrapper stays small and easy to test by injecting a MockTransport and a retrying instance.
  • Adopted despite: HTTPTransport's constructor options are not inherited, so create(**kwargs) has to forward them and type them separately (HTTPXHTTPTransportKeywordArguments).
  • Adopted despite: the wrapper must forward lifecycle methods such as close() / aclose() to the wrapped transport.

docs.title: Option 2: Subclass the HTTP transports
docs.text: Subclass httpx.HTTPTransport / httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport and override handle_request / handle_async_request to retry around the parent implementation.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: retrying would be tied to the HTTP transports and unavailable for other transport types, such as MockTransport or third-party transports.
  • Rejected because: it cannot be layered with other wrapping transports through composition.
  • Rejected despite: it inherits the constructor options and the close() / aclose() lifecycle for free, leaving one object to configure.

docs.title: Supporting Material
docs.text: • httpx transports documentation https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/transports/

docs.title: ADR003 - Configure retries with a retry policy protocol
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-11-07
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The transports' create() factories take a policy that implements the RetryPolicy protocol instead of individual retry arguments. The transport calls the policy's create() method with the tenacity retrying class it needs, its HTTP client's request error and its own logger. The default policy, SmartRetryPolicy, is a NamedTuple that holds the retry settings, including the status codes and header that smart_wait reads.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: TenaciousTransport.create() and AsyncTenaciousTransport.create() each took five retry arguments and repeated the same tenacity configuration. Settings added later, such as smart_wait's status codes and header, could only be reached through create() by adding them to both factories. The planned httpx2 integration doubles the number of factories. It also needs each transport to retry its own client's request error, because httpx2.RequestError is not a subclass of httpx.RequestError. Passing the wrong exception does not fail; connection errors are simply no longer retried. Users who need full control can already pass a tenacity retrying instance to a transport's constructor, so create() remains the place where sensible defaults are applied, as in ADR001.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) A retry policy protocol with a default NamedTuple policy
  2. Retry arguments on create() with a shared private helper
  3. A policy value consumed by the transport constructor
  4. A retry strategy with separate sync and async builders

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): A retry policy protocol with a default NamedTuple policy
docs.text: RetryPolicy is a Protocol with one method, create(retrying_class, *, request_error, logger), which returns an instance of the given tenacity.Retrying or tenacity.AsyncRetrying class. SmartRetryPolicy implements it with the previous defaults. Each transport's create() accepts a policy, defaults to SmartRetryPolicy(), and passes its own retrying class, request error and module logger.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: one policy object configures both the sync and the async transport, and will configure the transports of both HTTP clients.
  • Adopted because: the transport supplies the retrying class and request error it knows, so users cannot pair a policy with the wrong mode or client.
  • Adopted because: retry logs keep each transport's logger name, because the transport passes its own logger.
  • Adopted because: new settings become policy fields with defaults instead of new arguments on every create().
  • Adopted because: a custom policy only needs a matching create() method, which mypy and ty check structurally.
  • Adopted because: SmartRetryPolicy is a NamedTuple, the lightest-weight, truly immutable value object that Python provides.
  • Adopted despite: it is a breaking change to the signature of create().
  • Adopted despite: the protocol is a public contract, so changing the parameters of its create() breaks third-party policies.
  • Adopted despite: custom policies need the RetryingT type variable to annotate create(), so it becomes public API.
  • Adopted despite: a NamedTuple accepts positional arguments and compares equal to a plain tuple, so the documentation uses keyword arguments.

docs.title: Option 2: Retry arguments on create() with a shared private helper
docs.text: Keep the retry arguments on each create() and move the shared tenacity configuration into one private function.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: every new setting has to be added to the signature of each create(), four of them once httpx2 is supported.
  • Rejected because: the only way to customise retrying beyond those arguments is a complete tenacity retrying instance.
  • Rejected despite: it adds no public API and does not break callers.

docs.title: Option 3: A policy value consumed by the transport constructor
docs.text: Drop create(). The transport's __init__ accepts either a frozen, keyword-only dataclass of retry settings or a tenacity retrying instance, and builds the retrying instance and the default inner transport itself.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the constructor would build objects as a side effect instead of only storing what it is given.
  • Rejected despite: a keyword-only dataclass rejects positional arguments.
  • Rejected despite: users would configure the inner transport with the HTTP client's own constructor, so create() would no longer need to forward and type its keyword arguments.

docs.title: Option 4: A retry strategy with separate sync and async builders
docs.text: A RetryStrategy protocol with build_sync_retrying() and build_async_retrying() methods, and a default strategy that holds the retry settings, the retry predicate and the logging hook.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: every implementation has to provide both builders, even when it only serves one mode.
  • Rejected because: the strategy would choose the request error and the logger, although only the transport knows its HTTP client and logger.
  • Rejected despite: the method names make the mode explicit.

docs.title: ADR004 - Provide one integration per HTTP client
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-11-08
  • Status: ACCEPTED
  • Author: Moritz E. Beber

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: HTTPX becomes an optional dependency. The transports (TenaciousTransport, AsyncTenaciousTransport) and their keyword-argument TypedDict live in one sub-package per HTTP client, httpx_tenacity.httpx and httpx_tenacity.httpx2. Users select an integration explicitly by import, and each one is installed with the extra of the same name and guarded by an import error that names the extra. The client-independent core keeps its import paths: RetryPolicy, SmartRetryPolicy and RetryingT in the package root, and smart_wait and is_server_side_issue in httpx_tenacity.wait and httpx_tenacity.retry_callback. There is neither automatic client selection nor a compatibility alias for the old root imports.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: HTTPX2 is a separate package that keeps the HTTPX API but defines its own classes. Request, Response, Limits, Proxy, the transports and RequestError of one client are distinct types from those of the other. The two clients do not interoperate: an httpx.Client with an HTTPX2 transport, and the reverse, fails with an AssertionError. Users should be able to install the library with either client, or both, without pulling in the one they do not use. The retrying logic itself does not depend on any HTTP client. RetryPolicy and SmartRetryPolicy (ADR003) only build tenacity retrying instances, and smart_wait and is_server_side_issue only read the status_code and headers of a response, which a private structural Response protocol describes. Each transport passes its own client's RequestError to the policy, which is required because httpx2.RequestError is not a subclass of httpx.RequestError, so one policy can configure the transports of both clients. The transports follow ADR002 and subclass only their client's abstract base transport, so each integration needs its own sync and async classes. The package is still in pre-alpha, and the release that introduces the integrations already contains the breaking change to create() (ADR003), so a breaking change to the import paths is acceptable. The same decision was made for httpx-limiter, which this ADR adapts.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. (SELECTED) One integration package per HTTP client
  2. Select the HTTP client automatically
  3. One generic transport parametrized over the client
  4. Import aliasing so the same names come from either client
  5. Keep HTTPX required and add HTTPX2 only as an extra
  6. One integration package per HTTP client with compatibility aliases at the root

docs.title: Option 1 (SELECTED): One integration package per HTTP client
docs.text: Move the transports and HTTPXHTTPTransportKeywordArguments into httpx_tenacity.httpx and add httpx_tenacity.httpx2 with TenaciousTransport, AsyncTenaciousTransport and HTTPX2HTTPTransportKeywordArguments. Each package imports only its own client and never the other integration, annotates with that client's types, and raises a ModuleNotFoundError that names the extra to install when the client is missing. Other import errors are re-raised so that a missing transitive dependency is not hidden. The core in the package root imports no HTTP client.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adopted because: users install only the client they use, and tenacity is the only required dependency.
  • Adopted because: each integration is typed with its own client's classes, so type checkers reject mixing a transport, Limits or Proxy of one client with the other.
  • Adopted because: both integrations can be used in the same process, and one SmartRetryPolicy or custom RetryPolicy configures the transports of both.
  • Adopted because: both clients are treated symmetrically, so adding or dropping a client later does not move the other one.
  • Adopted because: the logger of each transport follows its module and therefore tells the retry logs of the two clients apart.
  • Adopted despite: the transport code exists twice, once per client, in sync and async variants, and every HTTP-facing change has to land in both.
  • Adopted despite: it is a breaking change. Every user must change the imports of the transports and the keyword-argument TypedDict and select an extra when installing.
  • Adopted despite: Limits and Proxy are client-specific types. The keyword-argument TypedDict and the create() signature therefore have to be defined per client, because mypy and ty reject a client-neutral protocol where create() forwards **kwargs to the client's transport.
  • Adopted despite: the loggers are renamed, for example from httpx_tenacity.tenacious_transport to httpx_tenacity.httpx.tenacious_transport. Logging configuration that targets the old names stops matching.
  • Adopted despite: the public classes exist twice under the same names, once per sub-package.

docs.title: Option 2: Select the HTTP client automatically
docs.text: Expose one set of transports in the root that use whichever client is installed, falling back from one to the other.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the choice is ambiguous when both clients are installed, and the result depends on the environment instead of the code.
  • Rejected because: the transports cannot be annotated with one client's types, so mix-ups would only fail at runtime with an AssertionError.
  • Rejected despite: users would not need to choose an import path.

docs.title: Option 3: One generic transport parametrized over the client
docs.text: Write the transport once and bind it to a client with class factories or generics, for example make_transport(httpx2).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the base transports, RequestError, Limits and Proxy are different classes in each client, so the class would have to be created at runtime and could not subclass the client's base transport in a way static checkers understand.
  • Rejected because: create() forwards the client's constructor arguments, whose Limits and Proxy types cannot be expressed without either client-specific code or a loss of type safety.
  • Rejected despite: the transport logic would exist only once.

docs.title: Option 4: Import aliasing so the same names come from either client
docs.text: Use one set of module-level names and rebind them to the other client's classes, for example with a conditional import.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: names that mean different classes depending on the environment hide which client is in use and defeat static typing.
  • Rejected because: it cannot serve both clients in the same process.
  • Rejected despite: the transport code would not be duplicated, and the call sites would look the same for both clients.

docs.title: Option 5: Keep HTTPX required and add HTTPX2 only as an extra
docs.text: Keep httpx as a required dependency and the transports in the package root, and add only httpx_tenacity.httpx2 behind a httpx2 extra.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: HTTPX2 users would still have to install HTTPX.
  • Rejected because: the two clients would be exposed asymmetrically, with one at the root and one in a sub-package.
  • Rejected despite: existing imports and installations would keep working without changes.

docs.title: Option 6: One integration package per HTTP client with compatibility aliases at the root
docs.text: Use the sub-packages from option 1, but keep the old root imports of the HTTPX transports as aliases.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rejected because: the root aliases must import HTTPX, so the root would no longer be client-independent, unless a lazy module __getattr__ is added, which complicates the core.
  • Rejected because: the package is in pre-alpha and the release already contains a breaking change, so a clean break is simpler for users and maintainers than a transition period.
  • Rejected despite: existing code would keep working for a transition period.
